title: Real-World Occurrence of Early-Onset Pulmonary Events in Patients with Advanced Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase-Positive (ALK+) Non-small Cell Lung Cancer Treated with Brigatinib: A Post-Authorization Safety Study.
authors: Hochmair MJ, Stewart G, Rauter M et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) and pneumonitis are known adverse events (AEs) with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs; e.g., brigatinib) that treat anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)+ non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In clinical trials, pulmonary events (e.g., ILD, pneumonitis, dyspnea, and hypoxia) occurring within 14 days of brigatinib initiation were termed early-onset pulmonary events (EOPEs). A step-up dosing regimen (180 mg daily following 7-day lead-in at 90 mg daily) reduced EOPE occurrence. Early-onset pulmonary events resemble symptoms of NSCLC and other lung diseases, complicating causality assessment. This post-authorization safety study evaluated EOPEs with brigatinib in a real-world setting.
METHODS: Adults with advanced ALK+ NSCLC starting brigatinib monotherapy were enrolled in this prospective, observational, single-arm, multicenter study. Pulmonary events during Days 1-14 were considered AEs of special interest (AESIs). An independent adjudication committee reviewed whether AESIs met EOPE criteria: (1) signs/symptoms began within 14 days after starting brigatinib, (2) evidence of a pneumonitis-like process, and (3) other etiology unlikely.
RESULTS: Among 98 patients, 90% received first-line brigatinib. Most (79%) started at 90 mg daily, later transitioning to 180 mg daily. Median relative dose intensity was 99.4%. Ten patients experienced 11 AESIs during the first 14 days of treatment; none were confirmed as EOPEs (0/98 patients; 0%; 95% CI 0.0-3.7%).
CONCLUSION: In this real-world study, most patients received the recommended dosage of brigatinib, and no EOPEs were confirmed after independent adjudication committee review. The relatively small sample size and different EOPE definitions should be considered when comparing these findings with clinical trials.
TRIAL REGISTRY: Clinical Trial Registration: europa.eu, EUPAS32383.

title: KIAA1217 in Human Disease: Emerging Evidence from Fusion Biology, Molecular Mechanisms, and Translational Perspectives.
authors: Wang Y, Qu C, Li N et al.
abstract: KIAA1217, also known as SKT or ETL4, was originally identified as a large, poorly characterized protein-coding gene and is increasingly implicated in human disease. Evidence is most developed in cancer, where KIAA1217 participates in fusions involving RET, FGFR2, and ALK. KIAA1217::RET has direct functional support in lung adenocarcinoma, activating ERK and PI3K/AKT signaling, whereas other fusions are supported mainly by sequencing and case-based observations. Independently, one experimental study indicated that KIAA1217 promotes hepatocellular carcinoma metastasis through JAK1/2-STAT3 signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Studies also implicate KIAA1217 in alternative splicing and multi-omics alterations, although these remain less mechanistically resolved. Beyond cancer, human genetic studies associate KIAA1217 with lumbar disc herniation and vertebral malformations. Experimental evidence for intervertebral disc development and synaptic organization derives primarily from murine Skt models and does not by itself establish equivalent functions of human KIAA1217. Other human and cross-species associations remain exploratory. This review integrates these findings using a multidimensional evidence framework and highlights unresolved links between KIAA1217 structural complexity and tissue-specific functions. Defining its interactome, disease-relevant isoforms, fusion-specific functions, and functional variants will be necessary to clarify KIAA1217-specific mechanisms and determine whether any of these findings have reproducible translational relevance.

title: Inhibition of ALK suppresses epithelial-mesenchymal transition in lung cancer cells by regulating TGF-β/SMAD signaling.
authors: Hu W, Sun Y, Wang S et al.
abstract: ALK-positive lung cancer represents a significant subset of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), characterized by insidious early symptoms, unfavorable prognosis, and high mortality, posing severe threats to patient quality of life and survival. We investigated the effect of crizotinib on epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in ALK-positive lung cancer cells by inducing EMT in H2228 cells through TGF-β1, and explored the mechanism of SMAD4 in this regulation by knocking down SMAD4. The mRNA expression of SMAD4 was quantified by qRT-PCR. Protein levels of E-cadherin and Vimentin were assessed via Western blot. Cellular invasive capacity was evaluated using Transwell assays. Cell migration potential was measured by scratch wound healing assays. SMAD4 nuclear translocation was visualized using immunofluorescence. qRT-PCR confirmed successful SMAD4 knockdown. Western blot analysis revealed that TGF-β1-induced EMT in NSCLC cells led to significant downregulation of E-cadherin and concurrent upregulation of Vimentin and p-SMAD2/3. Transwell assays demonstrated markedly enhanced invasiveness in EMT-induced cells, while immunofluorescence showed increased SMAD4 nuclear translocation. Crizotinib treatment effectively inhibited these TGF-β1-induced effects in H2228 cells, whereas the inhibitory effect was less pronounced in A549 cells. Scratch assays indicated that crizotinib reduced the enhanced migratory capacity of H2228 cells after EMT induction; however, this suppressive effect was attenuated following SMAD4 knockdown. Our findings demonstrate that crizotinib inhibits TGF-β1-induced EMT phenotypes and SMAD2/3 phosphorylation more prominently in ALK-positive NSCLC cells than in the ALK-negative counterpart. Crucially, SMAD4 ablation completely abolishes crizotinib's capacity to reverse EMT. These findings provide additional insight into the potential mechanism of crizotinib in NSCLC.

title: Pulmonary Large-Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma Combined With Adenocarcinoma Accompanied by Diffuse Idiopathic Pulmonary Neuroendocrine Cell Hyperplasia Tumours Distinguished From Multiple Pulmonary Metastases: A Case Report.
authors: Yamada T, Takahashi S, Yoshida N et al.
abstract: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH) is a rare pre-invasive lesion characterized by pathological neuroendocrine cell proliferation. We report a case of pulmonary large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) combined with adenocarcinoma and DIPNECH, in which differentiating DIPNECH from metastases was critical for accurate staging and treatment. A 68-year-old woman presented with a right upper-middle lobe mass and multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of nodules was performed for pathological diagnosis and genetic analysis. Nodules were diagnosed as DIPNECH tumours rather than metastatic lesions. Subsequently, a right middle lobectomy and right upper lobe segmentectomy were performed. The primary tumour was diagnosed as an LCNEC with pulmonary adenocarcinoma, staged as IIA (pT2bN0M0), accompanied by DIPNECH. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of combined LCNEC and adenocarcinoma accompanied by DIPNECH, illustrating that DIPNECH can mimic multiple pulmonary metastases and lead to overstaging.

title: Documented frequency of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome among patients with small cell lung cancer in a large United States health system.
authors: Chang CWM, Hidalgo L, Streicher NS
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is the paraneoplastic syndrome most often associated with small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Four published series in which unselected patients with SCLC were examined neurologically report LEMS in 1.3-3.8%; analyses of claims data report under 0.2%. We measured how often LEMS is documented among patients with SCLC in a large United States health system.
METHODS: In this retrospective cross-sectional study at MedStar Health, a 10-hospital academic health system, patients with SCLC were identified between May 24, 2019 and May 2025 by structured ICD-10 and chemotherapy-based queries (Arm 1A) and, because ICD-10 has no code specific to SCLC, by classifying oncology notes containing "small cell" with a large language model, every positive classification then confirmed against the note text (Arm 1B). Patients with LEMS were identified without date restriction using diagnosis codes, amifampridine orders, and text search, then adjudicated by chart review.
RESULTS: We identified 436 patients with SCLC (425 by text classification, 11 by structured query only) and 9 meeting a LEMS case definition (2 definite, 2 probable, 5 possible). No patient with SCLC diagnosed during the study period had a documented LEMS diagnosis (0/436; 95% CI 0-0.84%). One further patient with SCLC and possible LEMS was found only by the unrestricted search and died before the study period began. Seven of the nine had an associated malignancy (three NSCLC, one SCLC, one lymphoma, one astrocytoma, one breast) and four had died. A neurology encounter or electrodiagnostic study was mentioned in the index note of 18 of the 425 patients.
CONCLUSION: The documented frequency of LEMS in SCLC in routine care was zero, with an upper confidence bound below the lowest estimate from series that examined patients systematically. This is consistent with underrecognition, though the design cannot separate it from true absence of disease, care elsewhere, or incomplete documentation. Clinicians should consider LEMS when a patient with SCLC develops unexplained proximal weakness, hyporeflexia, autonomic symptoms, or bulbar complaints. The absence of a histology-specific code for SCLC, alongside a discrete code for LEMS, is itself a barrier to studying this question at scale.

title: Indoor Radon Concentrations and Associated Health Effects: A Review.
authors: Kuzmanović P
abstract: This paper presents a review of research on indoor radon concentrations in 27 countries worldwide, focusing on residential buildings, workplaces, schools, and kindergartens, as well as the health effects of long-term radon exposure. The analysis included radon measurements and epidemiological studies on the association between radon exposure and the risk of lung cancer. The results show significant regional variability in radon concentrations, influenced by geological characteristics, building age, construction materials, ventilation, and climatic factors. Concentrations ranged from <20 Bq/m3 to 56,000 Bq/m3. The highest values were recorded in Sweden, Norway, the Czech Republic, Serbia, Montenegro, Poland, Albania, Croatia, Hungary, and Slovenia, while lower concentrations were generally observed in some countries in Africa and Asia. Particularly elevated concentrations were recorded in schools and kindergartens, highlighting the need for systematic monitoring, especially among children. Epidemiological and cohort studies provide significant evidence of an association between radon and an increased risk of lung cancer. Meta-analyses indicate an increase in risk of approximately 5-15% for every 100 Bq/m3 increase in radon concentration, while estimates suggest that radon may be responsible for approximately 3-20% of lung cancer mortality and a significant proportion of cases among never-smokers. The synergistic effect of radon and smoking is particularly significant. Biological mechanisms include alpha radiation from radon progeny, DNA damage, oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic changes associated with carcinogenesis. Most epidemiological evidence supports a linear no-threshold relationship between radon and lung cancer risk, although some studies at concentrations <200-250 Bq/m3 have not demonstrated a statistically significant increase in risk. Debate regarding the effects of low concentrations continues, including the linear no-threshold model and the hypothesis of ionizing radiation-induced hormesis. Despite substantial evidence, gaps remain in knowledge and risk management. Epidemiological studies show heterogeneity in study design, measurement methodology, exposure assessment, and control of confounding factors, while radon potential maps and comprehensive monitoring are unavailable in many countries. In countries with elevated concentrations, risk management systems are often insufficiently developed. Standardized measurement procedures, continuous monitoring, improved mapping, harmonized exposure assessment, and more reliable epidemiological models are needed, together with strengthened national action plans and integrated strategies to reduce exposure and the associated health burden.

title: Cytoskeletal Gene Dysregulation in Exosomal Profiles as Prognostic Biomarkers for Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer Progression.
authors: Jahani MM, Mashayekhi P, Omrani MD
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is one of the major causes of cancer mortality worldwide. Even with improved therapy, the outlook is still poor because there are no useful biomarkers for early detection and therapeutic targets. Exosomes, being extracellular vesicles containing cytoskeletal components, are essential for cancer growth and metastasis. The purpose of this study is to detect significant cytoskeletal genes in NSCLC exosomes and evaluate their clinical relevance.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A bioinformatics approach was utilized to analyze gene expression profiles from the dataset GSE118370, including control and NSCLC samples. Genes involved in the function of exosomes and cytoskeleton elements were identified by Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses. Network Analyst was utilized to construct protein-protein interaction networks and clinical verification using The Cancer Genome Atlas and cBioPortal data. Survival analysis and the gene expression patterns were compared in order to determine the prognostic implication of these genes.
RESULTS: CDK1 and VCL were found to be upregulated significantly in NSCLC, and ACTA1 and CDH1 were downregulated. These genes were involved in cell cycle progression, cytoskeleton organization, and focal adhesion pathways. High expression of CDK1 and VCL had correlation with cancer stage at presentation and worse overall survival, whereas reduced ACTA1 and CDH1 expression had correlation with reduced survival.
CONCLUSION: Differential expression of cytoskeletal genes in NSCLC exosomes suggests their application as prognostic biomarkers and drug targets. Targeting these genes can provide novel strategies to improve patient outcomes and manage disease advancement in NSCLC.

title: Risk stratification of lung malignancy in a real-world LDCT cohort: implications for screening beyond smoking criteria in Taiwan.
authors: Lu CY, Lin SH, Chang YJ
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening has been widely implemented based primarily on smoking-related eligibility criteria derived from Western populations. However, lung cancer epidemiology differs substantially in Asia, where a considerable proportion of cases occur among never-smokers, particularly women. We aimed to identify clinical factors associated with lung malignancy detection in a real-world Taiwanese LDCT cohort in routine clinical practice and to explore the applicability of current smoking-based screening paradigms.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study including 7,319 adults who underwent LDCT between October 2018 and March 2023. Patients were categorized according to the LDCT referral pathway, and data on demographics, smoking history, comorbidities, and pathological outcomes were collected. Cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models were used for the outcome-specific analyses, with alternative mutually exclusive first pathological diagnoses censored at their diagnosis date and participants without a pathological diagnosis censored at their last available follow-up date.
RESULTS: During follow-up, 156 participants had pathological confirmation of lung malignancy. In the cause-specific Cox model using binary smoking status (Model 2), lung malignancy was significantly associated with female sex (adjusted HR 1.95, 95% CI 1.33-2.86), age ≥ 45 years (adjusted HR 3.81, 95% CI 2.19-6.63), smoking history (adjusted HR 2.48, 95% CI 1.47-4.18), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (adjusted HR 11.82, 95% CI 6.46-21.63). Notably, a substantial proportion of lung cancer cases occurred in non-smokers, particularly women. In contrast, family history was not consistently associated with overall lung malignancy detection but was associated with specific pathological subtypes.
CONCLUSIONS: In this real-world LDCT cohort, factors associated with lung malignancy detection included older age, female sex, smoking history, and COPD, with a notable burden among non-smoking women. These findings warrant further prospective studies to evaluate whether demographic and clinical factors could complement current smoking-based eligibility criteria in Asian populations.

title: Predicting Early Mortality After Whole-Brain Radiotherapy in Metastatic NSCLC to Support Patient-Centred Decision-Making.
authors: Bock F, Zettl H, Frerker B et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study sought to evaluate 30- and 60-day mortality following palliative whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) in patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and to identify readily accessible clinical predictors to guide therapeutic decisions.
METHODS: This retrospective single-centre study analyzed 392 patients treated with WBRT. Pretreatment factors were assessed using multivariable Cox regression and translated into the six-point Bedside Early Mortality Score (BEMS). The score's ability to predict mortality within 30 and 60 days of WBRT completion was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and compared with Lung-specific Graded Prognostic Assessment (Lung GPA) and Recursive Partitioning Analysis (RPA).
RESULTS: Overall, 115 patients (29.3%) died within 30 days and 178 (45.4%) within 60 days. The score included four parameters readily available during bedside consultation: age ≥65 years, direct inpatient transfer, and abnormal mental status at initiation of WBRT each contributed one point, while impaired mobility contributed three points. Each additional point increased the risk of mortality by 55% (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.46-1.64). Thirty- and sixty-day mortality according to score were, respectively, 2.2% and 8.5% (0-1 points), 10% and 36.7% (2-3 points), 57.8% and 85.7% (4-5 points), and 85.8% and 90.5% (6 points). Areas under the ROC curve for 30- and 60- day mortality were 0.855 and 0.881, compared with 0.685 and 0.740 for Lung GPA and 0.833 and 0.899 for RPA.
CONCLUSIONS: The Bedside Early Mortality Score may complement clinical evaluation and support shared decision making in WBRT. Independent validation is required.

title: The Role of Hospital Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical-Care Interventions in the Personalized Management of Patients with Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer: A Scoping Review.
authors: Nikolova N, Aleksandrov T, Yordanova M et al.
abstract: Background: Patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) increasingly receive oral targeted therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors, creating complex medication-management and toxicity-monitoring needs. Pharmacists may contribute through medication optimization, adherence support, patient education, drug-interaction management and multidisciplinary toxicity prevention. Objectives: The objectives of this study were To systematically map the published evidence describing pharmacist and pharmaceutical-care roles relevant to medication safety, adherence, toxicity management, and treatment continuity in NSCLC. Methods: A scoping review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science, supplemented by citation and supplementary searching. The search was limited to English-language publications published between 28 August 2016 and 28 August 2026. After reconciliation, 481 unique records were screened. Eligibility was assessed against a NSCLC-specific population and pharmacy/pharmaceutical-care concept criteria. Evidence was classified as core/direct or contextual/supporting. The selection process was reported according to PRISMA-ScR. Results: Of 481 unique records screened, 444 were excluded at title/abstract screening and 37 reports underwent an eligibility assessment. Twenty-three were excluded at this stage, leaving 14 sources of evidence: 11 core/direct and three contextual/supporting sources. Core evidence covered medication optimization and drug-drug interactions, adherence monitoring, adverse-event/toxicity management, patient education, and pharmacist-led ambulatory or multidisciplinary services. Conclusions: Pharmacists contribute meaningfully to medication safety, adherence, toxicity management, and treatment continuity in NSCLC, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous. Larger prospective studies and economic evaluations are needed.

title: Impact of multimedia scenarios on students' perceptions and discussion tendencies in problem-based learning: a comparative study of three sequential cohorts among Japanese medical students.
authors: Abe Y, Jego EH, Maruoka S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: While textual cases are common in problem-based learning (PBL), students often find it difficult to fully understand patient conditions on the basis of text alone. In this study, multimedia and text-based PBL scenarios were compared with respect to students' perceived understanding of patient conditions and their consideration of differential diagnoses.
METHODS: In this comparative study of three sequential cohorts, from 2021 to 2023, third-year medical students at Nihon University School of Medicine participated in PBL sessions featuring three diseases, namely, Parkinson's disease, lung cancer, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, using either text-based or multimedia scenarios. Multimedia elements included medical interview videos, auscultation sounds, and computed tomography (CT) imaging videos. A total of 123, 114, and 118 students were enrolled in 2021, 2022, and 2023, respectively. After each PBL session, the students completed a survey and submitted a report. The topics selected in these reports were analysed and categorized into the following three categories: symptoms, physical and diagnostic findings, and differential diagnoses.
RESULTS: In the Parkinson's disease scenario, which entailed the presentation of visible symptoms such as tremors and gait abnormalities, 83% of the students reported that they could understand the patient's condition, significantly more than for lung cancer (58%) or hypersensitivity pneumonitis (53%). Introducing multimedia elements such as auscultation sounds and CT imaging videos was significantly associated with a higher proportion of students who selected differential-diagnosis topics in the lung cancer scenario (p < 0.05) and the hypersensitivity pneumonitis scenario (p < 0.01). Moreover, the addition of multimedia medical interviews appeared to be associated with different patterns of student responses according to disease characteristics, with greater perceived understanding observed for Parkinson's disease and broader consideration of differential-diagnosis topics observed for lung cancer and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tutors also generally reported that students could understand the patient's condition in the multimedia scenarios.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with traditional text-based formats, multimedia scenarios were associated with greater perceived understanding of patient conditions and broader consideration of differential-diagnosis topics. For diseases with prominent physical features such as Parkinson's disease, multimedia medical interviews were particularly associated with students' perceived understanding of patient conditions. For diseases identified mainly through imaging or auscultation, such as lung cancer and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, multimedia elements were associated with broader consideration of differential-diagnosis topics. These findings suggest that the use of multimedia in PBL may be associated with students' perceived understanding of patient conditions and broader consideration of differential-diagnosis topics during PBL discussions.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable. This study did not involve a clinical trial.

title: Recurrent Hepatic Metastasis of Occult Type B1 Thymoma with Multifocal Spread: A Rare Case Report and Literature Review.
authors: Luo Y, Wei P, Qiao L et al.
abstract: Thymoma is a rare tumor of thymic epithelial cells, accounting for 20-30% of mediastinal tumors. It typically grows slowly and remains confined to the anterior mediastinum, with distant metastasis, such as to the liver, being extremely rare. Liver metastasis and recurrence are particularly rare in type B1 thymoma, making clinical diagnosis more challenging. We report the case of a 60-year-old female who presented with right upper quadrant pain, and imaging revealed a large liver mass. She underwent hepatic bisegmentectomy of S4b and S5 and cholecystectomy, with postoperative pathology confirming hepatic type B1 thymoma. Further evaluation identified a soft tissue mass in the anterior-superior mediastinum, leading to right anterior mediastinal tumor resection and right middle lobectomy, with pathology again confirming type B1 thymoma. The patient received adjuvant chemotherapy. Four years later, tumor recurrence prompted diaphragmatic, paraspinal, and pulmonary nodule resections. Another recurrence occurred after 4 years, necessitating a left hemihepatectomy, which revealed recurrent type B1 thymoma in the liver. She remains recurrence-free during postoperative follow-up. Type B1 thymoma presenting with hepatic metastasis as the initial manifestation is exceedingly rare. Despite its conventionally favorable prognosis, aggressive biological behavior including hematogenous dissemination and multifocal recurrence may occur. Aggressive surgical resection, including repeat hepatectomy in selected patients, may prolong survival. Long-term abdominal surveillance and multidisciplinary management are strongly recommended for such patients.

title: [Advances in pathologic diagnosis and updates in classification and grading of pleural mesothelioma].
authors: Fu QS, Mei W, He B
journal: Zhonghua Lao Dong Wei Sheng Zhi Ye Bing Za Zhi
abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PMe) is a primary malignant tumor originating from pleural mesothelial cells, characterized by high invasiveness, rapid progression and poor prognosis. Its occurrence closely associated with asbestos exposure. The diagnosis of pleural mesothelioma presents several challenges in diagnostic pathology, as each histological subtype has its own unique differential diagnosis. No single antibody is completely sensitive or specific for mesothelioma; instead, the diagnosis relies on a combination of several antibody panels. The most commonly mutated genes in pleural mesothelioma are BAP1, CDKN2A, and NF2.Accurate diagnosis and evaluation of pleural mesothelioma typically require a multimodal approach, combining cytological testing, CT scans, and MRI imaging. This article comprehensive reviews the pathological diagnosis and differential diagnosis of PMe, interprets the relevant updates in the 2021 WHO classification of thoracic tumors. It synthesizes and summarizes the clinicopathological features of pleural mesothelioma, including the main differential diagnoses, diagnostic pitfalls, and criteria for distinguishing benign from malignant lesions. Furthermore, the article reviews the latest advancements in molecular genetic research on mesothelioma, exploring the involved pathogenesis and diagnostic methods. It also reviews the prognostic indicators associated with this disease. By providing these insights, the article offers valuable guidance for both the pathological diagnosis and clinical management of mesothelioma.

title: [Research progress on the application of microRNA in the clinical diagnosis and prognostic evaluation of pleural mesothelioma].
authors: Cheng X, Li ZL, Xiong W
journal: Zhonghua Lao Dong Wei Sheng Zhi Ye Bing Za Zhi
abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is a rare, a highly aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis. PM occurs more frequently in individuals with a history of long-term asbestos exposure and is characterized by a long latency period, atypical early symptoms and a high rate of misdiagnosis. microRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of small non-coding RNAs that regalate gene expression post-transcriptional. Aberrant miRNA expression is closely associated with tumorigenesis, progression and metastasis, and miRNA can be detected in serum, plasma, pleural effusion, tumor tissues and extracellular vesicles. This review outlines the biogenesis and functions of miRNAs, systematically summarizes advances in miRNAs research on the early diagnosis, differential diagnosis and prognostic evaluation of PM, and discusses the challenges retated to detection standardization, clinical validation and translational application. Current evidence indicates that combined detection of multiple miRNAs may improve diagnostic efficacy, and specific miRNA expression profiles can also be used for survival risk stratification. miRNAs hold promise as novel biomarkers for the early diagnosis and prognostic evaluation of PM.

title: Cystic clear cell thymoma in a cat: clinical, imaging, anatomopathological and immunohistochemical findings.
authors: Maia LVP, Serakides R, Pastor FM et al.
abstract: Thymomas are uncommon thymic epithelial neoplasms in cats and may present uncommon histological variants, such as cystic clear cell thymoma. The aim of this case report was to describe the clinical, imaging, anatomopathological, and immunohistochemical findings of a cystic clear cell thymoma in a four-year-old mixed-breed female cat presented with anorexia and progressive dyspnea. Imaging examinations revealed a large heterogeneous mediastinal mass with cystic components, accompanied by pleural effusion and pulmonary compression. Ultrasound-guided cytology was inconclusive. Despite intensive supportive care, the patient died due to respiratory failure. Necropsy revealed a large mediastinal mass occupying approximately 70-80% of the thoracic cavity, accompanied by compressive pulmonary atelectasis and hydrothorax. Histologically, the neoplasm was predominantly composed of carbohydrate-rich clear epithelial cells accompanied by cystic structures, scattered mature lymphocytes and rare Hassall's corpuscles. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong nuclear expression of p40, p63 and CKAE1/AE3 in the neoplastic cells, whereas CD3 labeling was restricted to non-neoplastic lymphocytes, supporting the diagnosis of cystic clear cell thymoma. This report expands the current knowledge of this rare tumor variant in cats and highlights the importance of imaging examinations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry for establishing a definitive diagnosis.
